title: Who pays for AI power - the data-center-to-ratepayer cost shift (PJM capacity spike + large-load tariffs)
source: Public record: PJM capacity-auction results; Monitoring Analytics (Joseph Bowring, PJM independent market monitor); NRDC; PA/OR/VA PUC orders; Harvard Salata (Peskoe/Martin); Fortune/IEEFA. National/systemic macro overlay (structural; no financial-core edges). HONESTY: PJM prices + Monitoring Analytics data-center attribution = fact; NRDC cumulative + per-household estimates = advocacy projections (reported); the cost-shift MECHANISM (rate case -> PUC allocation) = fact; 'consumers subsidize AI' = a real structural dynamic, magnitude graded.

edges.notes: Data-center load drove ~63% of PJM's 2025/26 capacity-price increase (~$9.3B, per Monitoring Analytics/Bowring); the 2028-29 auction cleared at the FERC price cap ($325/MW-day, ~$16.4B total, ~$6.3B data centers) even as supply fell ~6.8GW short - a ~$30B cumulative data-center burden across recent auctions (fact).

PJM capacity prices went ~11x ($28.92 -> $329.17/MW-day, 24-25 -> 26-27), hitting the cap two auctions running; NRDC estimates $100-163B cumulative ratepayer cost through 2033 absent intervention, ~$70/month/household by 2028; DC Pepco bills +$21/mo (June 2025), about half from capacity (fact on PJM prices; NRDC/per-household = reported estimates).
PJM is the largest US grid operator (~67M people, IL to VA/DC); its ~3-year forward capacity auctions mean today's data-center-driven prices are already locked into coming bills (fact).

FERC approves the capacity price cap + interstate transmission cost allocation; PUCs then divide those costs among ratepayers - the two-layer process that lets data-center costs socialize absent a special rate class (fact of structure).

The core cost-shift: when a utility builds generation/transmission for a large new data center, the PUC decides who pays; without a dedicated rate class those costs historically spread across ALL ratepayers - and special data-center contracts are often shielded as proprietary, hiding the shift (mechanism = fact; 'consumers subsidize AI' magnitude = graded).

The regulatory fix: as of Jun 2026, 24 states approved large-load tariffs making data centers cover their own interconnection/infrastructure costs (Dominion VA GS-5, Oregon Schedule 96/PGE, Texas SB6, Ohio AEP, PA statewide model for >50MW individual / 100MW aggregate); the White House added a 'Ratepayer Protection Pledge' (fact).

Large-load tariffs aim to shield existing residential/small-business ratepayers from data-center cost-shifting - but reform stalled regionally: PJM stakeholders voted down all major cost-allocation proposals (Nov 2025), leaving it to the PJM Board; 'the devil is in the details' of utility-specific filings (fact of tariffs + the gridlock).

Rising bills are a core driver of the local + political data-center backlash - fueling moratoria, siting fights, and the ratepayer-protection push (fact of dynamic; interpretation of causation weight).
